USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the G20 pause intact and press the talks that just reopened in Beijing. Do not hike List 3 from 10% to 25% while mid-level negotiations are live, and do not trade the March deadline for a purchase-only package. Use the remaining weeks to force written, enforceable movement on IP, forced tech transfer, and non-tariff barriers, treating extra farm/energy buys as a down payment, not the deal.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but not high. Combined Section 301 coverage is already ~$250B, and China has matched with tariffs on ~$110B of US goods, including soybeans, autos, and aircraft (timeline 2018-07-06, 2018-08-23, 2018-09-24). That retaliation has already bitten a politically sensitive export sector: US soybean shipments to China in Jan–Oct 2018 were 63% below a year earlier, with USDA projecting weaker FY2019 ag exports and a large Market Facilitation Program needed to offset farm losses. US macro is not in crisis, but it is no longer costless: Michigan sentiment fell to 91.2 in January from 98.3 in December, VIX is still ~20 after the December spike, 10-year yields have dropped from the autumn 3.2% area to 2.74%, and customs imports from China are down ~14% from the late-2018 peak. The Meng Wanzhou arrest on the same day as the G20 dinner, and China’s subsequent detention of two Canadians, add a hostage/tech overlay that can spoil a commercial settlement if it is folded into the tariff talks. That is a +0.2 threat reading: material sectoral and market stress, not a recessionary or existential hit.

Action should stay at negotiate (0.0), not escalate and not concede. The Dec 1 truce already bought the only new US leverage that matters right now—the suspended Jan 1 hike of List 3 to 25% if no agreement is reached in 90 days—and Beijing is showing it feels the pressure: China’s 2018 equity wipeout, first industrial-profit drop in three years, contracting manufacturing PMI, and slower official growth have coincided with Liu He dropping into the Jan 7 working-level talks, restarted soybean purchases, and discussion of larger US goods buys. Escalating tariffs or another ZTE-style non-tariff blow now would likely collapse a channel that just reopened and invite broader retaliation into US supply chains and farm states. A purchase-only or partial-rollback concession would repeat the May 19 “trade war on hold” episode that collapsed ten days later when structural 301 issues were left open. Lighthizer’s brief is still the right one: keep the hike as a backstop, refuse empty purchase promises, and spend the rest of the window on enforceable structural text.
key_factors: 90-day G20 truce still live; List 3 remains at 10% with a March hike backstop
Jan 7 Beijing working-level talks reopened; Liu He attended; purchases discussed, structural issues still open
US farm retaliation is the main domestic cost (soy to China down sharply; USDA aid already required)
US financial/sentiment conditions have tightened (UMCSENT 91.2, post-December vol, falling 10Y) but growth is not breaking
China is under more cyclical stress than the US, which is the source of current US leverage
Meng arrest plus Canadian detentions raise the cost of mixing law-enforcement/tech cases into a tariff bargain

sources_cited.excerpt: G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended. Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou.
Trade talks resume in Beijing (working / mid-level). China discusses increased purchases of US goods; structural issues remain open.
List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B.
Joint statement after talks: China agrees to significantly increase purchases. Mnuchin says trade war is on hold. Truce later collapses when the US proceeds with 301 tariffs.
University of Michigan consumer sentiment latest 91.2 on 2019-01-01, down 5.0 points / ~5.2% in the window, after 98.3 in December.
VIX latest 19.98 on 2019-01-09 after a December spike to 36.07; still well above mid-2018 teens.
US goods imports from China latest 41303 mil. $ in Jan 2019, down ~13.6% from the window start and off the Oct peak of ~52081.
US soybean exports to China for January through October 2018 are 63% lower than during the same period in 2017; USDA forecasts weaker FY2019 ag exports and deployed a large farm aid package.
Jan 7 working-level talks open in Beijing; Liu He dropped by; Gerrish leading the US team; Lighthizer-Liu meeting possible if there is progress.
Lighthizer is trying to keep Trump from accepting empty purchase promises and wants structural changes on forced tech transfer and IP before the March 2 deadline.
China GDP growth moderated to 6.5% in Q3; equities down ~20% and RMB ~6% vs USD; World Bank projected 6.2% growth in 2019.
